guideTitle: Best Leaf Vacuum Mulchers for Small Yards (2026)
metaTitle: Best Leaf Vacuum Mulchers for Yards
metaDescription: Compare six electric leaf vacuum mulchers by CFM, MPH, mulch ratio, impeller material, bag size and battery or cord, with advice for small and medium yards.
expertTake: The WORX Trivac WG588.1 is the top pick because it combines 600 CFM with a stated 20:1 mulch ratio and triple-layer metal impellers on a 40V battery. The corded WORX WG509 is the value pick for a small yard near an outlet. Skip the category if your yard is mostly paved or has few leaves, because a plain blower and a rake cost less and store smaller.
introParagraphs: A leaf vacuum mulcher is a three-in-one yard tool: you blow leaves into a pile, switch to vacuum mode to suck them up, and an impeller shreds them into a bag. Shredded leaves take far less room than whole ones and can go straight on garden beds or into a compost bin.

For small and medium yards, the details that matter are airflow in CFM, the stated mulch ratio, whether the impeller is metal or plastic, bag size, and whether power comes from a cord or a battery. This guide compares those and what changes in daily use.

products.name: WORX Trivac WG588.1 40V Cordless 3-in-1, 600 CFM, 20:1 Mulch
products.description:
The WORX WG588.1 is a 40V cordless three-in-one with up to 600 CFM of airflow, 100 MPH air speed and a stated 20:1 mulch ratio. The listing says robust triple-layer metal impellers produce fine mulch, and the tool switches from blower to vacuum without tools.

The tradeoff is air speed. At 100 MPH, it moves bulk leaves well but is weaker on stuck debris than the 210 MPH WORX WG509. Compared with the EGO LV5000 at 500 CFM and 16:1, it has more airflow and a higher mulch ratio, but it is the second most expensive of the nine candidates. Compared with the MZK at 700 CFM, it states a more detailed impeller build.

In ownership, the impeller is the wear part. Clear jams with the battery removed, empty the bag before it packs tight and check the impeller edges for nicks each season. A cordless design is limited by battery runtime, so confirm which battery and charger are included before buying.
products.bestFor: Yards of small to medium size where bag volume and fine mulch matter.
pros: Up to 600 CFM gives strong bulk airflow for moving large piles of leaves
Stated 20:1 mulch ratio is the highest in this group for compact bags
Triple-layer metal impellers resist wear better than plastic blades
Tool-free switch from blow to vacuum mode saves time between tasks
cons: 100 MPH air speed is far below the 210 MPH of the corded WORX models
Second most expensive of the nine candidates, with battery runtime as a limit

products.name: EGO Power+ LV5000 Leaf Vacuum Mulcher, 500 CFM, 16:1, Tool Only

specList.label: Air speed
specList.value: Up to 210 MPH with tapered nozzle

specList.label: Included
specList.value: Tool only, battery and charger not included

products.description:
The EGO LV5000 is a battery tool with a 40L heavy-duty bag, a six-blade metal impeller at a 16:1 mulch ratio, and a blower rated up to 500 CFM and up to 210 MPH with the tapered nozzle attached. The listing says it is sold without the battery and charger.

The tradeoff is that you must already own, or buy, an EGO battery and charger, which can add a lot to the cost. Compared with the WORX WG588.1, it has less airflow at 500 CFM but much higher air speed. Compared with the WORX WG583, it has more CFM and a higher mulch ratio, and it uses a more premium platform.

In ownership, a six-blade metal impeller should last well, but check it for nicks. The 40L bag is easy to empty, and the shared battery lets you run other EGO tools. If you do not own the platform, the real price is the tool plus a battery.
products.bestFor: People who already own EGO batteries and want a strong yard tool.
pros: Six-blade metal impeller gives a stated 16:1 mulch ratio for compact bags
Blower reaches up to 210 MPH with the tapered nozzle, good for stuck debris
40L heavy-duty bag is easy to empty and stays in shape
Shares batteries with other EGO outdoor tools, which saves cost
cons: Sold tool only, so the battery and charger are an extra cost
500 CFM is lower than the WORX WG588.1 and MZK airflow numbers

products.name: MZK 40V Brushless Leaf Vacuum Mulcher, 700 CFM, 40L Bag
products.description:
The MZK is a 40V brushless leaf vacuum mulcher that claims up to 700 CFM and 180 MPH, with a 40L bag and an anti-jam design. The listing mentions an internal suction tube meant to stop clogging at the joints and a turbo mode that runs for short bursts.

The tradeoff is that these are the maker's headline figures and the brand is less established than WORX or EGO. Compared with the WORX WG588.1, it claims more CFM and more air speed, but the listing does not state a mulch ratio in our data. Compared with the Greenworks blower, it is a three-in-one tool.

In ownership, the anti-jam tube is a useful idea since clogging is the main complaint with vacuum tools. Remove the battery before clearing a jam, empty the bag often and check the connectors. Because the brand is smaller, check what battery and charger come in the box and what the warranty covers.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want the highest claimed airflow and an anti-jam design.
pros: Claimed 700 CFM is the highest airflow figure in this group
Brushless motor is described as efficient and long-lasting
Anti-jam suction tube is aimed at the clogging problem in vacuum mode
Fourth of nine in price, below the premium WORX and EGO systems
cons: Peak figures are maker claims and the brand is less established
No stated mulch ratio in the data we had, so bag reduction is unclear

products.name: WORX WG583 40V Brushless 3-in-1, 340 CFM, 210 MPH, 12:1
products.description:
The WORX WG583 is a 40V brushless three-in-one with 340 CFM, 210 MPH and a 12:1 mulch ratio. It is aimed at lawns, patios and driveways, replacing raking and bagging by hand.

The tradeoff is that its airflow and mulch ratio are below the newer WG588.1 at 600 CFM and 20:1. Compared with the corded WG509, it adds cordless freedom but costs more and offers the same 210 MPH. Compared with the EGO LV5000, it has lower CFM and a lower mulch ratio, but it is less costly and includes more of what you need in some listings.

In ownership, plan around runtime and keep a spare battery for a big yard. Empty the bag before it packs hard, wipe the intake and inspect the impeller for chips. A 12:1 ratio means more bags than a 20:1 model for the same pile of leaves.
products.bestFor: Cordless buyers who want WORX quality at a mid-range level.
pros: Cordless 40V brushless design avoids dragging a cord across the yard
210 MPH air speed is good for moving stuck leaves from lawns and corners
12:1 mulch ratio cuts bag volume noticeably compared with unmulched leaves
Sixth of nine in price, below the premium cordless systems
cons: 340 CFM and 12:1 are lower than the newer WORX WG588.1 numbers
Battery runtime limits larger yards unless you add a second battery

products.name: WORX Trivac WG509 12 Amp Corded 3-in-1, 350 CFM, 210 MPH, 18:1
products.description:
The WORX WG509 is a corded 12 Amp three-in-one that delivers up to 350 CFM and 210 MPH, with an 18:1 mulch ratio. It is the cheapest of the nine candidates and is sold for lawns, patios and driveways.

The tradeoff is the cord. You are limited by an extension cord and an outlet, which suits small yards but frustrates anyone with a large lot. Compared with the WORX WG583, it matches the 210 MPH and offers a higher 18:1 ratio at a lower price, but with no cordless freedom. Compared with the WG588.1, it has less airflow but a similar mulch ratio class.

In ownership, a corded motor has no battery to replace, which is a plus for long-term cost. Use an outdoor-rated extension cord of the right gauge, keep it behind you and unplug before clearing jams. Check the impeller and the bag zipper each season.
products.bestFor: Small yards near an outlet where cost and mulch ratio matter most.
pros: Cheapest of the nine candidates with a stated 18:1 mulch ratio
No battery to buy, charge or replace, so long-term cost stays low
210 MPH air speed moves stuck debris from hard surfaces
12 Amp motor is a simple, proven design with few parts to fail
cons: Corded, so reach is limited by the outlet and a suitable extension cord
350 CFM is much lower than the cordless models with larger airflow

products.name: CRAFTSMAN 12 Amp Corded 3-in-1 Blower Vacuum Mulcher, 450 CFM
products.description:
The CRAFTSMAN is a corded 12 Amp three-in-one with up to 450 CFM and 260 MPH, plus tool-free conversion between blower, vacuum and mulcher. The listing describes a backpack-style bag for hands-free use.

The tradeoff is the corded design and the lack of a published mulch ratio in our data. Compared with the WORX WG509, it has more CFM, 450 against 350, and more air speed, 260 against 210, but it costs more and gives no ratio. Compared with the cordless EGO LV5000, it is cheaper and has no battery to buy, but you are tied to an outlet.

In ownership, use an outdoor-rated extension cord, keep the vacuum tube clear and check the bag for tears. Because the bag is a backpack-style design, the weight sits on your shoulders and it is easier to use for longer sessions.
products.bestFor: Corded buyers who want the highest airflow and speed from an outlet-powered tool.
pros: Up to 450 CFM and 260 MPH are the strongest corded numbers in this group
Tool-free conversion switches between blower, vacuum and mulcher quickly
Third of nine in price, low for a tool with this much airflow
Backpack-style bag spreads the weight and keeps hands free
cons: Corded design limits reach and needs a proper extension cord
No stated mulch ratio in our data, so bag reduction is unclear

buyingCriteria.explanation: The mulch ratio says how much shredding reduces volume, for example 20:1 on the WORX WG588.1 against 12:1 on the WG583. A higher ratio means fewer bag trips. Bag size also matters: a 40L bag, as on the EGO and MZK, fills fast. Buyers often compare ratio and ignore how often they will have to empty the bag.

CFM measures air volume and moves bulk leaves, while MPH measures speed and lifts stuck debris. The MZK claims 700 CFM and 180 MPH, while the WORX WG588.1 offers 600 CFM and 100 MPH. For wet leaves on a lawn, volume and speed both help. Peak figures are the maker's, not an independent test.

The impeller shreds the leaves, and metal wears slower than plastic. The WORX WG588.1 lists triple-layer metal impellers, and the EGO uses six metal blades. Plastic impellers can crack on twigs and acorns. Check the material before you buy if your yard has many branches.

Corded models like the WORX WG509 and CRAFTSMAN have no runtime limit but need an outlet. Battery models give freedom but limited runtime, which drops fast at full power. A yard larger than a quarter acre usually needs a second battery or a cord.

Vacuum mode clogs when wet leaves pack into the tube. The MZK lists an anti-jam internal tube, and wide, smooth tubes help on all models. Clearing a clog often means removing the battery or unplugging. Take this seriously, since jams are the top frustration.

A leaf vacuum carries the weight of the bag, motor and battery. A backpack-style bag, as on the CRAFTSMAN, spreads the load. A shoulder-strap bag is lighter but tiring over a large yard. Try to judge weight from the listing and your own strength.

specDecoder.meaning: CFM is the volume of air moved per minute. Higher CFM pushes more leaves at once.
specDecoder.watchFor: The MZK claims 700 CFM and the WORX WG588.1 lists 600, but these are peak maker figures.

specDecoder.meaning: MPH is how fast the air leaves the nozzle. It helps lift wet or stuck leaves.
specDecoder.watchFor: The WORX WG509 and WG583 list 210 MPH, and the WG588.1 lists only 100 MPH.

specDecoder.meaning: A ratio such as 20:1 means the shredder reduces leaf volume to a twentieth. A higher ratio means fewer full bags.
specDecoder.watchFor: The WG588.1 lists 20:1, the WG509 18:1, the EGO 16:1 and the WG583 12:1.

specDecoder.meaning: Battery tools use volts, such as 40V, and corded tools use amps, such as 12 Amp. They are not directly comparable.
specDecoder.watchFor: The WORX WG509 and CRAFTSMAN are 12 Amp corded, and the others are 40V.

specDecoder.meaning: Bag size in liters or bushels sets how often you stop to empty. A larger bag is heavier when full.
specDecoder.watchFor: The EGO and MZK list a 40L bag, and many listings do not give a size.

howWeEvaluated.title: Airflow and speed
howWeEvaluated.description: We evaluated the stated CFM and MPH from the published listings, from 340 to 700 CFM and from 100 to 260 MPH. These are maker peak figures, and we did not measure any tool.

howWeEvaluated.title: Mulching performance
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared stated mulch ratios and impeller materials. The WORX WG588.1 lists 20:1 with metal impellers, and the EGO lists 16:1 with six metal blades. Some listings give no ratio.

howWeEvaluated.title: Power and runtime
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared corded and cordless designs. Corded tools like the WG509 avoid runtime limits, and cordless tools need a battery, so we noted where the battery is not included.

howWeEvaluated.title: Handling and bag
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered bag size, backpack design and anti-jam features from the listings. The MZK lists an anti-jam tube and the CRAFTSMAN a backpack-style bag.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership and value
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at wear parts like impellers and batteries, from owner feedback patterns. We weighed price position against what is included, since a tool-only EGO costs more once a battery is added.

cards.label: Corded
cards.text: The WORX WG509 and CRAFTSMAN have no runtime limit and no battery to buy. They are cheaper, but you need an outlet and a cord to manage.

cards.label: Cordless
cards.text: The WG588.1, WG583, MZK and EGO give freedom to roam, but runtime is limited and a second battery adds cost.

howToChoose.note: Choose corded for a small yard near power and cordless if you need to move around a larger space.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A modest CFM, a good mulch ratio, a light bag and easy storage. A small yard rarely needs 700 CFM, and a corded tool can be the better value.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The WORX WG509 and WG583 are the best fits for small yards, and the CRAFTSMAN suits a corded yard with more debris.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You have a medium or large yard, want fewer bag trips and plan to use a battery platform for other tools, as with the WORX WG588.1 or EGO.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You have a small yard near an outlet. The WORX WG509 costs the least and offers a strong mulch ratio.

maintenance.why: Damp mulch left in the bag grows mold and clogs the mesh. Shake it out and let it dry.
Wet leaves and twigs jam the impeller. Always remove the battery or unplug the tool before clearing a jam.
Nicks or bent blades reduce mulching and cause vibration. Replace worn impellers per the maker's guidance.
Lithium batteries age faster when stored hot or fully drained. Store them partly charged at room temperature.
A frayed cord or loose connector is a hazard. Replace damaged cords and keep connectors dry.

faq.q: Is corded or cordless better for a leaf vacuum mulcher?
faq.a: Corded tools avoid runtime limits and cost less, but you need an outlet. Cordless tools give freedom but run for a limited time at full power. Pick by yard size and distance from power.

faq.q: How much should I spend on a leaf vacuum mulcher?
faq.a: The corded WORX WG509 and CRAFTSMAN cost the least. Spend more for cordless freedom, higher airflow or a high mulch ratio. A tool-only EGO adds the cost of a battery.

faq.q: How long do the impellers last?
faq.a: Metal impellers wear slower than plastic, but twigs and stones can nick them. No listing states a rated lifespan. Inspect each season and avoid sucking up stones.

faq.q: Does a higher mulch ratio mean a better tool?
faq.a: It means fewer bags for the same leaves, but it does not guarantee a finer or more even result. Ratios are maker claims, so use them as a guide, not a measurement.
Wet leaves are heavy and clog tubes and impellers. Most tools work better on dry leaves, and wet leaves slow the machine. Let them dry a day if you can.
Yes. Electric leaf vacuums are quieter than gas tools but still loud enough to need ear protection, and eye protection is wise. Follow local noise rules for use hours.
